quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: The vocabulary of standards, price variances and efficiency variances for materials and labour.

questions.q: A price variance measures:
options: The difference between actual and standard quantity of input, valued at standard price
The difference between actual and budgeted price of an input, applied to the actual quantity used
The difference between actual and budgeted units of output
The change in selling price of the product
questions.explain: Price variance = (actual price − budgeted price) × actual input. The first option describes the efficiency variance.

questions.q: An efficiency variance measures:
options: Whether the mill paid more than standard for cloth
Whether more or less input was used than the standard allows for the actual output, valued at the budgeted price
The number of jackets sold below budget
questions.explain: Efficiency variance = (actual input − budgeted input allowed for actual output) × budgeted price. Paying more per unit is the price variance.

questions.q: The price variance plus the efficiency variance of an input equals that input's flexible-budget variance.
questions.explain: For Webb's materials, 22,200 U price + 66,000 U efficiency = 88,200 U flexible-budget variance. The two parts fully explain the gap between actual cost and the flexible budget.

questions.q: What does 'budgeted input allowed for actual output' mean for Webb's cloth?
options: 2 yd per jacket × 12,000 jackets budgeted = 24,000 yd
2 yd per jacket × 10,000 jackets actually made = 20,000 yd
questions.explain: The standard quantity is flexed to the actual output of 10,000 jackets: 20,000 yd. Using the budgeted 12,000 jackets would mix in the volume effect.

questions.q: A standard cost per unit of output is built from:
options: Standard input per unit × standard price per input
Actual input per unit × actual price
questions.explain: For cloth: 2 yd × Rs 30 = Rs 60 per jacket; for manufacturing labour 0.8 h × Rs 20 = Rs 16.

questions.q: In this lecture's sheet the heading says 'U = positive'. A price variance of 22,200 for materials therefore means:
options: Webb paid Rs 22,200 less than standard — favourable
Webb paid Rs 22,200 more than standard — unfavourable
Webb used 22,200 yd more than standard
questions.explain: Positive is unfavourable in this sheet (the opposite of lecture 13's convention): Rs 31 instead of Rs 30 on 22,200 yd. The quantity used was 22,200 yd, a coincidence of numbers.

questions.q: The marketing labour line shows price variance 2,304 U and efficiency variance (4,704) F. In words:
options: Marketing staff were paid less per hour and worked more hours
Marketing staff were paid more per hour but worked fewer hours than the standard allows
Marketing staff were paid more and worked more
questions.explain: Rs 25 instead of Rs 24 per hour (U) but 2,304 h instead of the 2,500 h allowed (F); the net is 2,400 F.

questions.q: The efficiency variance is valued at the actual price so that it reflects what was really spent.
questions.explain: It is valued at the budgeted (standard) price; otherwise the price effect would be counted twice. Only the price variance carries the actual price.

questions.q: In a spinning mill, the lecture says the price and efficiency split separates:
options: 'Cotton got dearer' from 'we wasted more cotton'
questions.explain: A rise in cotton price is a purchasing matter; using more cotton per lb of yarn is a mill-floor efficiency matter. Mixing them in one figure hides who is responsible.

questions.q: Which of these is a direct input to a jacket in Webb's standards?
options: Direct manufacturing labour at 0.8 h per jacket
questions.explain: The three inputs analysed are cloth (2 yd), manufacturing labour (0.8 h) and marketing labour (0.25 h), each with a standard price.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Which formula gives which variance, and which way it moves when prices or quantities change.

questions.q: The price variance for an input is calculated as:
questions.explain: The price difference is applied to the quantity actually bought or used: (31 − 30) × 22,200 = 22,200 U for cloth. Actual cost − flexible budget is the total flexible-budget variance.

questions.q: The efficiency variance for an input is calculated as:
options: (Actual input − budgeted input allowed for actual output) × budgeted price
(Actual input − budgeted input allowed for actual output) × actual price
questions.explain: The quantity difference is valued at the standard price: (22,200 − 20,000) × 30 = 66,000 U. Using the actual price would double-count the price change.

questions.q: Actual price Rs 31 per yd, budgeted Rs 30, actual usage 22,200 yd. What is the materials price variance?
Actual usage 22,200 yd, standard 2 yd per jacket, 10,000 jackets made, budgeted price Rs 30 per yd. What is the materials efficiency variance?
questions.explain: Allowed = 20,000 yd; (22,200 − 20,000) × 30 = Rs 66,000 unfavourable.

questions.q: If the actual price of an input falls below standard while usage is unchanged, the price variance becomes:
questions.explain: A negative (actual − budgeted) price makes the price variance favourable; the efficiency variance is unaffected because it uses the budgeted price.

questions.q: The actual quantity of cloth used rises but the price paid stays at standard. Which variance changes?
questions.explain: With actual price = budgeted price the price variance is zero whatever the quantity; the extra yards appear entirely in the efficiency variance.

questions.q: The flexible-budget cost of an input equals the budgeted input allowed for actual output multiplied by the budgeted price.
questions.explain: Cloth: 20,000 yd × Rs 30 = Rs 600,000; manufacturing labour 8,000 h × Rs 20 = Rs 160,000; marketing labour 2,500 h × Rs 24 = Rs 60,000.

questions.q: Standard manufacturing labour is 0.8 h per jacket at Rs 20. What is the flexible-budget labour cost for 10,000 jackets?
questions.explain: 8,000 h allowed × Rs 20 = Rs 160,000. Actual was Rs 198,000, a flexible-budget variance of 38,000 U.

questions.q: If output had been 12,000 jackets instead of 10,000 with the same actual inputs, the materials efficiency variance would:
options: Become favourable, because 24,000 yd would be allowed and only 22,200 were used
questions.explain: Allowed input rises to 2 × 12,000 = 24,000 yd; (22,200 − 24,000) × 30 = 54,000 F. The efficiency variance always depends on the output actually achieved.

questions.q: Which of these events shows up in the cloth efficiency variance rather than the price variance?
options: Negotiating a lower price per yard
A better marker that uses fewer yards per jacket
Buying a dearer quality of cloth
questions.explain: Yards per jacket is a quantity matter, valued at the standard price in the efficiency variance. The other three change the price paid per yard and appear in the price variance.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Webb's three inputs, then the same split applied to a spinning mill's cotton.

questions.q: Webb used 22,200 yd of cloth costing Rs 688,200. What was the actual price per yard?
questions.explain: 688,200 ÷ 22,200 = Rs 31.00 per yard, Rs 1 above the Rs 30 standard.

questions.q: Manufacturing labour: 9,000 hours cost Rs 198,000; the standard is Rs 20 per hour. What is the labour price variance?
questions.explain: Actual rate 198,000 ÷ 9,000 = Rs 22; (22 − 20) × 9,000 = Rs 18,000 unfavourable.

questions.q: Manufacturing labour: 9,000 hours used, standard 0.8 h per jacket at Rs 20, 10,000 jackets made. What is the labour efficiency variance?
questions.explain: Allowed 8,000 h; (9,000 − 8,000) × 20 = Rs 20,000 unfavourable. Together with 18,000 U price this gives the 38,000 U flexible-budget variance.

questions.q: Marketing labour: 2,304 hours cost Rs 57,600; standard Rs 24 per hour. What is the price variance?
questions.explain: Actual rate 57,600 ÷ 2,304 = Rs 25; (25 − 24) × 2,304 = Rs 2,304 unfavourable.

questions.q: Marketing labour: 2,304 hours used, standard 0.25 h per jacket at Rs 24, for 10,000 jackets. What is the efficiency variance? (Favourable as a negative number, following the sheet's U = positive convention.)
Materials flexible budget Rs 600,000, actual cost Rs 688,200. What is the materials flexible-budget variance?
questions.explain: 688,200 − 600,000 = Rs 88,200 unfavourable = 22,200 U price + 66,000 U efficiency.

questions.q: A spinning mill's standard is 1.25 lb of cotton per lb of yarn at Rs 150 per lb. In a month it used 13,000 lb of cotton costing Rs 2,015,000 to make 10,000 lb of yarn. What is the cotton price variance?
questions.explain: Actual price 2,015,000 ÷ 13,000 = Rs 155; (155 − 150) × 13,000 = Rs 65,000 unfavourable — 'cotton got dearer'.

questions.q: Same mill: 13,000 lb of cotton used for 10,000 lb of yarn, standard 1.25 lb per lb at Rs 150. What is the cotton efficiency variance?
questions.explain: Allowed 12,500 lb; (13,000 − 12,500) × 150 = Rs 75,000 unfavourable — 'we wasted more cotton'.

questions.q: Webb's three inputs show flexible-budget variances of 88,200 U, 38,000 U and 2,400 F. What is the combined flexible-budget variance for these three inputs?
questions.explain: 88,200 + 38,000 − 2,400 = 123,800 U. The 130,000 U in lecture 13 covered all variable costs including overheads; 128,600 wrongly adds the favourable marketing variance.

questions.q: Standard cloth is 2 yd per jacket. Webb used 22,200 yd for 10,000 jackets. What was the actual cloth per jacket?
questions.explain: 22,200 ÷ 10,000 = 2.22 yd per jacket, 0.22 yd (11 %) above standard.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Who is responsible for which variance, and what the numbers tell a mill or garment manager to do.

questions.q: Webb's cloth shows a 22,200 U price variance and a 66,000 U efficiency variance. Which department should be asked about the larger problem?
options: Production, about the 2,200 extra yards used
questions.explain: The efficiency variance (Rs 66,000) is three times the price variance; the cutting room used 2.22 yd per jacket instead of 2. Purchasing answers for the Rs 1 per yard.

questions.q: The purchasing manager bought a cheaper cloth, giving a favourable price variance, but cutting wastage rose and the efficiency variance became unfavourable. How should management judge this?
options: Look at the two variances together: a cheaper cloth that causes more wastage may cost more overall
Change the standard to the cheaper cloth
questions.explain: Price and efficiency variances are often linked; a decision in one department can cause a variance in another, so the net flexible-budget variance and the cause must be examined.

questions.q: A favourable labour efficiency variance always means workers were more productive.
questions.explain: Fewer hours can also come from skipping inspection, rushing work or an out-of-date standard; the marketing labour 4,704 F should be investigated like any other variance.

questions.q: A spinning mill shows a cotton price variance of 65,000 U and an efficiency variance of 75,000 U. Which action addresses the efficiency variance?
options: Reducing waste in blow room and carding so less cotton is used per lb of yarn
Changing the standard price to Rs 155
questions.explain: Efficiency is about the quantity of cotton per lb of yarn; waste control on the floor reduces it. Contracts address the price variance.

questions.q: Webb's manufacturing labour rate was Rs 22 against a Rs 20 standard. Which explanation would make this variance NOT the production manager's fault?
options: Overtime was worked to catch up lost production
A general wage award negotiated by head office raised all rates
Workers were idle during a machine breakdown
questions.explain: A company-wide wage rise is outside the production manager's control; overtime, skill mix and idle time are operating matters.

questions.q: Marketing labour cost Rs 57,600 against a flexible budget of Rs 60,000 — 2,400 F overall. A manager says 'no need to look further'. What is the weakness in that view?
options: The variance is unfavourable, not favourable
The net figure hides a 2,304 U price variance and a 4,704 F efficiency variance that may have different causes
Marketing labour is a fixed cost
questions.explain: A small net variance can be the sum of two larger opposite effects; the split shows staff were paid more per hour but worked fewer hours.

questions.q: A garment unit sets its cloth standard at 2 yd per jacket but the marker (cutting layout) actually needs 2.1 yd. What will the variance report show month after month?
options: A recurring unfavourable efficiency variance of 0.1 yd per jacket that is really a wrong standard
questions.explain: A standard that cannot be achieved produces a permanent U efficiency variance; the right response is to investigate and, if the 2.1 yd is genuine, revise the standard.

questions.q: Cotton prices rise sharply mid-month. In the variance report this appears mainly as:
options: An unfavourable price variance, because actual price exceeds the standard on all cotton used
questions.explain: The market price change is applied to the actual quantity used; quantity per lb of yarn is unaffected unless the mill also changed its waste.

questions.q: Calculating the efficiency variance at the budgeted price lets management compare efficiency across months even when input prices change.
questions.explain: Valuing quantity differences at a constant standard price isolates usage from market movements, so a 2,200 yd overuse is always Rs 66,000 at the Rs 30 standard.

questions.q: A costing office wants to use price and efficiency variances in a weaving mill. For yarn consumption the 'input allowed for actual output' would be:
options: Standard yarn per metre × metres actually woven
Standard yarn per metre × metres budgeted
Actual yarn issued to the looms
questions.explain: Exactly as for Webb's cloth: standard usage per unit of output flexed to the actual output. Budgeted metres would reintroduce the volume effect.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step problems, sign conventions and common slips in splitting the flexible-budget variance.

questions.q: A student computes Webb's materials efficiency variance as (22,200 − 20,000) × 31 = 68,200 U. What is the error?
options: The allowed quantity should be 24,000 yd
The efficiency variance must use the budgeted price of Rs 30, giving 66,000 U; using Rs 31 double-counts the price change
The actual quantity should be 20,000 yd
questions.explain: With the actual price, price + efficiency would be 22,200 + 68,200 = 90,400, which no longer equals the 88,200 U flexible-budget variance.

questions.q: A mill's standard is 1.25 lb of cotton per lb of yarn at Rs 150. It made 10,000 lb of yarn from 13,000 lb of cotton costing Rs 2,015,000. What is the total cotton flexible-budget variance?
questions.explain: Flexible budget = 12,500 lb × 150 = Rs 1,875,000; actual Rs 2,015,000; variance Rs 140,000 U = 65,000 U price + 75,000 U efficiency.

questions.q: Webb's materials price variance is 22,200 U on 10,000 jackets. If the same Rs 1 per yard price rise applied to the standard 2 yd per jacket, what would the price variance have been?
questions.explain: 1 × 20,000 yd = Rs 20,000. The extra Rs 2,200 arises because the price rise is paid on the 2,200 yd of overuse too — a joint price-and-quantity effect that convention assigns to the price variance.

questions.q: In lecture 13 Webb's variances were shown with 'positive = F'; in this lecture the sheet uses 'U = positive'. The materials variance of 88,200 would therefore appear as:
options: (88,200) in lecture 13's convention and 88,200 here, both meaning unfavourable
questions.explain: The sign convention is a presentation choice; the economic meaning is the same. Always read the sheet's note before interpreting a sign.

questions.q: Standard manufacturing labour is 0.8 h per jacket at Rs 20. Webb used 9,000 h at Rs 22 for 10,000 jackets. If the labour rate had stayed at Rs 20, what would the flexible-budget labour variance have been?
questions.explain: 180,000 − 160,000 = Rs 20,000 U: with no price variance the whole flexible-budget variance is the efficiency variance.

questions.q: Marketing labour: actual 2,304 h at Rs 25; standard 0.25 h per jacket at Rs 24; 10,000 jackets. Which statement is correct?
options: Price 2,304 U, efficiency 4,704 F, net 2,400 F
Price 2,304 F, efficiency 4,704 U, net 2,400 U
Price 2,500 U, efficiency 4,704 F, net 2,204 F
Price 2,304 U, efficiency 4,704 F, net 7,008 U
questions.explain: (25 − 24) × 2,304 = 2,304 U; (2,304 − 2,500) × 24 = 4,704 F; net 2,400 F (57,600 vs 60,000). The third option wrongly uses the allowed hours in the price variance.

questions.q: Suppose Webb had made 11,000 jackets using the same 22,200 yd at Rs 31. Standard 2 yd at Rs 30. What would the materials efficiency variance be? (Unfavourable positive, favourable negative.)
questions.explain: Allowed 22,000 yd; (22,200 − 22,000) × 30 = Rs 6,000 U. The price variance would stay at 22,200 U because it depends on actual yards, not output.

questions.q: If actual price equals standard price and actual usage equals the allowed usage, both variances are zero but the flexible-budget variance can still be non-zero.
questions.explain: Price + efficiency = flexible-budget variance, so if both parts are zero the flexible-budget variance is zero too: actual cost equals standard quantity × standard price.

questions.q: Webb's total standard cost per jacket for the three inputs is 60 + 16 + 6 = Rs 82. Actual cost of the three inputs was 688,200 + 198,000 + 57,600 for 10,000 jackets. What was the actual cost per jacket for these inputs, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 943,800 ÷ 10,000 = Rs 94.38 per jacket against Rs 82 standard — Rs 12.38 per jacket, matching the 123,800 U combined variance.

questions.q: A mill reports a cotton price variance of 65,000 U and an efficiency variance of 75,000 U, but the costing office then finds the standard price should have been Rs 155, not Rs 150. After correction the variances become:
questions.explain: Actual price Rs 155 equals the corrected standard, so the price variance vanishes; the efficiency variance is revalued at Rs 155: 500 lb × 155 = Rs 77,500 U. A wrong standard shifts variances between the two parts.
